segment:
Adrian looked down at the covered object in his palm, and said to Mara, “Well, that was quick. Thank you.” Then he closed his own hand over hers, smiled, and stood back up straight again, leaving her palm on his. He reached under her other hand and picked up the remaining two objects.

He handed one of them to Jonah, who accepted it in his right hand and put it back down beside the plastic cup. With the third object in his left hand, he returned to his place in front of the couch, his right arm still covered over by Mara’s palm.
“And now?” she asked, lifting her right hand away.
Adrian took it and turned it palm-up in front of him. “This is yours, I believe,” he said, holding it out to her.

Mara looked down at the brass key lying there on his palm, then up at him, and back down at the key. “Yes. Yes, thank you.” She accepted it and held it carefully in both hands for another long moment, looking at it; then she looked back up at the man who’d given it to her.

Adrian was watching her face. He turned and gave a small nod to Jonah, who placed the token beside his cup on the table as Adrian picked up the stone from his palm. “Your turn,” he said to Jonah, handing over the stone. Jonah accepted it. Mara took a step closer toward Jonah as Adrian began walking toward the doorway.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

And that was when a door opened down the hallway behind her, releasing two voices into the room. One female, one male; one asking a question, the other replying; neither loud nor excited, just casual conversation. Jonah released her hand and turned away to look down the hall at them.
When Mara heard the voices and followed his gaze, she saw one young man who wasn’t Jonah, but close in size and shape; he had brown hair and a beard and was carrying a glass.

The brown-haired man glanced once over his shoulder, saw them standing there, nodded hello, and stepped right into the gathering, holding up his glass of wine—a half-full plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo on it. “Cheers.” He set it on the table against the wall to the left of the door, and stepped forward to shake Jonah’s hand as they exchanged names.

As he set down the glass and moved out of its space, a previously unseen catering worker entered from the hallway behind him and retrieved it. She wore the same black-and-white striped Fulcrum uniform shirt, though she looked old enough to have had that job since the Institute was founded; and she gave no outward sign of the social fact that she was taking their discarded drink back to the kitchen, while the rest of the conversation went on.

Mara watched this woman return to the hallway where she belonged, and noticed herself noticing who assumed whose labor.

“It is a glass of wine,” he said, looking at Mara. “An ordinary plastic cup, such as is now being handed out by that woman, carrying wine in it. If you see anything different, you may certainly tell us.” His gaze still on hers, he placed his right hand flat against the table beside them and said to Jonah, “Hold this, will you?”
Jonah picked up the cup. “Do I want the contents first?”
Adrian waved that aside. “We won’t break the cup, don’t worry.” He held up his left hand, palm outward, toward Mara, and placed three objects in her open palm: a brass key, a white stone, and a wooden token.
Mara looked down at his hand, then up into his eyes, waiting to see what was wanted next.
“Choose one of those three,” he said. “Silently, please. Which one will you keep?” He smiled, leaned closer, and said, “You don’t have to answer right now, mind; but if you don’t want to play at all, we should stop.”

Mara considered for a moment. She wasn’t sure what this game proved, except for the fact that she had agreed to play it, though it seemed simple enough. “I will play,” she said quietly, and looked down at the objects again.

She examined each one carefully. The key was brass, or maybe copper, with no teeth but a wide bow; it might once have been part of a toy, but was now worn and unidentifiable. The white stone felt like limestone to her, weathered smooth, flat on top. And the token looked like the kind they used in a local arcade back home: she remembered them as round wooden chips with numbers printed in blue, though this one was blank.

Mara considered them for another long moment, looking down at her palm. She closed her eyes, and then opened them again, and then—without looking at Adrian—placed one of the three in the palm of his left hand and covered it over with her other hand. “There,” she said.

Adrian looked down at the covered object in his palm, and said to Mara, “Well, that was quick. Thank you.” Then he closed his own hand over hers, smiled, and stood back up straight again, leaving her palm on his. He reached under her other hand and picked up the remaining two objects.

He handed one of them to Jonah, who accepted it in his right hand and put it back down beside the plastic cup. With the third object in his left hand, he returned to his place in front of the couch, his right arm still covered over by Mara’s palm.
“And now?” she asked, lifting her right hand away.
Adrian took it and turned it palm-up in front of him. “This is yours, I believe,” he said, holding it out to her.

Mara looked down at the brass key lying there on his palm, then up at him, and back down at the key. “Yes. Yes, thank you.” She accepted it and held it carefully in both hands for another long moment, looking at it; then she looked back up at the man who’d given it to her.

Adrian was watching her face. He turned and gave a small nod to Jonah, who placed the token beside his cup on the table as Adrian picked up the stone from his palm. “Your turn,” he said to Jonah, handing over the stone. Jonah accepted it. Mara took a step closer toward Jonah as Adrian began walking toward the doorway.

segment:
“You can tell me whether you think I chose rightly.”
He didn’t immediately remove his hand to check her answer. He waited long enough for her to wonder; and then, he looked around for something to do next. Mara let him choose.

Continued manuscript
“And now—yes? Shall we move on?” He gave one final look around the room, as if expecting someone else to appear or make an objection; and then smiled at Mara again, and nodded, and swept his hand past Jonah to gesture toward the chairs.

“Now we’ll do the same game with this.”
Adrian had stepped past her into the space by the couch, and was holding the cup in one hand and a small wooden box in the other; he opened the lid and withdrew one last item, setting the box aside as he did so. “It is a coin,” he said to Jonah, who was still holding the wineglass with his right hand while watching Mara, and passed the coin into his outstretched palm.

Mara took one of the chairs near the table and sat down, still watching them carefully; the new object looked like an ordinary quarter-dollar coin to her, shiny in his hand, and she saw no need for any other description yet. The coin was not what Adrian had brought her attention to in the first place.
He took it in both hands, one on each side, and asked, “Are you ready?”

Jonah answered quickly. “Yes.”
“Good. And remember that the object is for the two of us to be aware of each other’s actions without interfering. Are we clear about that?”

segment:
“Which one?”

She looked up at Adrian’s face as she asked him to name the object; he nodded back and said, “We’ll find out together, then.” He drew the palm of his left hand across the table toward the plastic cup Jonah was still holding. “Jonah?” he prompted.
“Oh!” Jonah pulled his right hand back. “Wait—”

Before anyone could say anything else, another female voice spoke up from the doorway to Mara’s left—not the worker from earlier, but a different voice. She turned that way, saw a slim brown woman leaning in through the open doorway and looking up at her; she had to crane her neck upward to look the girl in the face.
Mara looked down into that face. The newcomer had short dark hair, a strong mouth, and eyes so dark they looked almost black in contrast with the pale blue circle around them; they were also—she noticed almost at once, as their gazes met—looking directly past her left ear, so the woman appeared to be looking straight at Mara but was in fact not making any kind of eye contact at all.

“I’m Livia,” she said, and held out a hand in greeting, palm down toward her knee. “Nice to meet you. May I help with something?” She smiled at her words, though her smile didn’t seem directed toward Mara in particular—it might just as easily have been at any of them.

“Livia, this is Mara,” Jonah said as Mara returned the handclasp. “She’s interested in seeing the Institute.”
Mara felt herself blush, and looked up toward Adrian’s face to find his eyes still on Jonah and Livia, not looking at her.
